items.prompt: Why does water have to turn into vapour before it can rise into the sky as part of the water cycle?

options.label: Because liquid water cannot be lifted by air, but scattered molecules can
options.feedback: Once water has scattered into separate, light molecules, moving air is able to carry it upward the way it never could a whole body of liquid.

options.label: Because vapour weighs nothing at all
options.feedback: Water vapour still has mass; it rises because it behaves differently from liquid, not because it has none.

options.label: Because the sun burns the water away
options.feedback: Nothing is destroyed by sunlight here; the water is not consumed, only changed in form.

options.label: Because clouds pull water up like a magnet
options.feedback: No pulling force reaches down from above; water has to leave the surface under its own power first.

items.ok_line: A liquid can't fly, but its molecules can.
items.ko_line: Ask what changes about the water itself, not what happens above it.
items.exp_text: A body of liquid water is held together by molecules clinging to their neighbours, far too heavy and bound together to be lifted by moving air. Heat gives some of those molecules enough energy to break free of that grip one at a time and drift off as invisible vapour, light and separate enough for air currents to carry upward. Only once the water has scattered into that gas can it begin the climb back into the sky.

items.prompt: What makes rising water vapour turn back into tiny liquid droplets high in the sky?

options.label: The vapour freezes solid immediately
options.feedback: Freezing would make ice, not the liquid droplets that actually form; cold slows the molecules first, it does not always freeze them.

options.label: The vapour cools down and its molecules slow enough to stick together
options.feedback: As molecules lose energy they move more slowly, and slow molecules are easily held together by the weak attraction between them.

options.label: The vapour becomes too heavy to stay a gas
options.feedback: A gas molecule's weight never changes; what changes is how it behaves once it slows down enough to cling to others.

options.label: Sunlight pushes the vapour molecules together
options.feedback: Sunlight adds energy and keeps molecules apart; the coming-together happens as that energy is lost, not gained.

items.ok_line: Cooling is a brake, and slow molecules stick.
items.ko_line: Something has to change about how fast the molecules are moving.
items.exp_text: Water vapour is made of molecules moving fast and independently, too energetic to hold onto each other. As that vapour rises into cooler air, the molecules lose energy and slow down, and once they are slow enough the weak attraction between them is enough to make them stick on contact. Groups of stuck-together molecules build into the tiny droplets that begin the next stage of the cycle.

items.prompt: How does water locked deep in the soil find its way back into the sky without ever evaporating off bare ground?

options.label: It seeps sideways until it reaches a river
options.feedback: That path takes water to the sea eventually, not up into the air.

options.label: Underground heat boils it upward
options.feedback: There is no heat source underground driving this; the soil is usually cooler than the surface, not hotter.

options.label: Plant roots draw it up and leaves release it as vapour
options.feedback: Roots pull water up through the stem, and any surplus escapes as vapour through the leaves, lifting soil water into the air a plant at a time.

options.label: It clings to falling raindrops and gets carried back up
options.feedback: Rain only ever falls; nothing about a falling drop can carry water upward with it.

items.ok_line: A plant works like a straw with an open top.
items.ko_line: Something living is doing the lifting here, not gravity or heat.
items.exp_title: A plant as a hidden pump
items.exp_text: Roots draw water out of the soil to feed the plant, and far more comes up than the plant actually keeps. The surplus travels up through the stem and escapes as vapour through openings in the leaves, a process called transpiration. Soil water that might otherwise stay trapped underground gets lifted into the sky this way, riding a plant the whole way up.

items.prompt: Why do the droplets inside a cloud eventually fall as rain instead of staying suspended forever?

options.label: They run out of water to hold
options.feedback: A droplet doesn't run dry; the issue is weight, not a shortage inside it.

options.label: The wind stops blowing beneath them
options.feedback: Wind and rising air are not the same thing, and calm air alone would not make a droplet fall; weight is what decides that.

options.label: Sunlight evaporates the air around them
options.feedback: If the air itself evaporated there would be nothing left for the droplet to fall through; the mechanism has to work on the droplet, not the air.

options.label: They join together until they are too heavy for rising air to hold up
options.feedback: Each merger adds weight without adding extra lift, and eventually gravity overcomes the rising air that had been keeping the droplet suspended.

items.ok_line: Enough small drops make one that gravity wins.
items.ko_line: Think about what changes about the droplet itself as it grows.
items.exp_title: A tug of war the droplet eventually loses
items.exp_text: Tiny cloud droplets are light enough for rising currents of air to hold them up rather than let them fall. As droplets bump into each other while drifting around inside the cloud, they merge into fewer, larger drops, and each merger adds weight without adding much extra push from below. Once a drop grows heavy enough that gravity beats the air holding it up, it falls, and that fall is what reaches the ground as rain.

items.prompt: What happens to rainwater that soaks into open soil instead of running off downhill?

options.label: It seeps down through gaps between soil and rock particles into stores underground
options.feedback: It trickles from one tiny gap to the next, drawn down by its own weight, until it collects underground.

options.label: It stays exactly where it landed forever
options.feedback: Water in soil keeps moving; it does not freeze in place once it soaks in.

options.label: It evaporates instantly the moment it touches soil
options.feedback: Soaking in and evaporating are opposite directions; water that has gone down cannot also leave upward at the same instant.

options.label: It turns into a gas that plants breathe
options.feedback: Plants use water as a liquid drawn up by roots, not as a gas taken in the way air is.

items.ok_line: Soil is full of tiny gaps, and water finds every one.
items.ko_line: Follow the water downward, not up or sideways.
items.exp_text: Soil and the rock beneath it are never perfectly solid; they are laced with tiny gaps and pores between particles. Water that soaks in trickles down through those gaps under its own weight, moving from one pore to the next until it collects in a saturated layer underground. That underground store keeps rivers and wells fed long after the rain that caused it has stopped falling.

items.prompt: Why does rain sometimes flow across the surface of the ground instead of soaking in?

options.label: Because rain always prefers flat ground
options.feedback: Water has no preference; whether it soaks in or flows depends on the ground, not the rain.

options.label: Because the ground is already full or too packed for more water to enter
options.feedback: Once the gaps in the soil are full or the surface is packed too tight, incoming rain has nowhere to go but sideways down the slope.

options.label: Because the ground is too cold for water to enter it
options.feedback: Temperature is not what blocks water from soaking in; a packed or already-soaked surface is.

options.label: Because sunlight pushes the water sideways
options.feedback: Sunlight adds heat, not sideways motion; nothing about light moves water horizontally.

items.ok_line: A soil with no room left sends water elsewhere.
items.ko_line: Ask what would stop water going down rather than what pushes it sideways.
items.exp_title: When the ground has no room left
items.exp_text: Soil can only absorb water as fast as its gaps can carry it downward, and once those gaps are full or the surface is packed too tight, no more water can enter. Rain that keeps falling after that point has nowhere to go but sideways, pulled by gravity down the nearest slope. That surface flow, called runoff, is what fills streams and rivers during and after a storm.

items.prompt: What powers the entire water cycle, lifting water off oceans and lakes in the first place?

options.label: The spin of the Earth
options.feedback: Spinning moves air and water sideways around the planet, but it supplies no energy to turn liquid water into vapour.

options.label: Pressure from the deep ocean
options.feedback: Deep water is under great pressure, but pressure pushes water together; it does not send any of it upward as vapour.

options.label: Heat energy from the sun
options.feedback: Turning liquid water into vapour takes energy, and that energy arrives as heat from the sun warming the surface.

options.label: Cold air sinking from high altitude
options.feedback: Sinking cold air settles low and stays there; nothing about it reaches down to lift water off a surface.

items.ok_line: Every rising drop first borrowed some of the sun's heat.
items.ko_line: Something has to add energy before any water can leave a surface as vapour.
items.exp_text: Turning liquid water into vapour takes energy, since molecules have to be given enough of a push to break away from the water around them. That energy arrives as heat from the sun, warming oceans, lakes and soil and setting the whole upward half of the cycle in motion. Cut off the sun's heat and the evaporating would stop, however much water was still sitting on the surface waiting to rise.

items.prompt: Why does rain fall as fresh water even though most of it evaporated from the salty sea?

options.label: The salt evaporates too, but falls back down first
options.feedback: If salt evaporated with the water, rain would taste salty; nothing filters it back out before it falls.

options.label: Rain clouds are made from a different, unsalted part of the ocean
options.feedback: Evaporation happens across the whole surface of the sea; there is no unsalted patch it draws from instead.

options.label: The sun burns the salt away completely
options.feedback: Salt is not destroyed by sunlight; it is left behind in the sea, not eliminated.

options.label: Salt is too heavy and bonded to lift into vapour with the water
options.feedback: Salt is held in the water by strong bonds, far too strong to be carried off in the same gentle escape that lifts water molecules alone.

items.ok_line: Only the water itself makes the climb.
items.ko_line: Think about what leaving the surface as vapour actually requires.
items.exp_text: Evaporation only lifts individual water molecules that gain enough energy to break free and drift off as gas. Salt is made of ions held in the water by much stronger attractions, far too strongly bonded to be carried off in the same gentle escape. So the vapour rising off the sea is pure water alone, and every raindrop that falls from it carries none of the salt it left behind.

items.prompt: Roughly how much new water does the water cycle create as it moves water from sea to sky to land and back?

options.label: None: the same water is recycled again and again
options.feedback: Every stage moves water around; none of them build a water molecule out of anything else, so the total supply just keeps being reused.

options.label: A little more each year as ice melts
options.feedback: Melting ice moves existing water from one form to another; it does not add water that did not already exist.

options.label: A large amount, replaced by water vapour from the sun
options.feedback: The sun supplies energy, not matter; nothing about sunlight adds actual water molecules to the cycle.

options.label: A small amount, made deep underground
options.feedback: Underground stores hold existing water that soaked in from above; nothing down there manufactures new water.

items.ok_line: The same molecules, over and over.
items.ko_line: The cycle moves water around; ask whether anything actually makes more of it.
items.exp_text: Evaporation, condensation and rainfall only ever move water from one place and form to another; none of the steps builds a water molecule out of anything else. The total amount of water on Earth has stayed essentially fixed for as long as the cycle has been running, just endlessly reshuffled between ocean, air, ice and land. A drop that once fell as rain long before you were born could easily be part of the water you drink today.

items.prompt: How can a patch of snow shrink on a cold, dry, sunny day even though the temperature never rises above freezing?

options.label: It melts too fast to notice
options.feedback: Melting needs the temperature to reach the freezing point from below; this is happening while it stays below freezing the whole time.

options.label: Ice turns directly into vapour without ever becoming liquid
options.feedback: Molecules at the ice surface can gain enough energy to break free straight into vapour, skipping the liquid stage entirely.

options.label: Wind blows the snow away as tiny particles
options.feedback: Blown snow just moves to a new pile somewhere else; the total amount of snow does not actually shrink that way.

options.label: The snow compacts into a smaller, denser pile
options.feedback: Compacted snow still contains the same amount of water; nothing has actually left it, only its shape has changed.

items.ok_line: Solid straight to gas, no liquid stop in between.
items.ko_line: The temperature never crosses the melting point, so melting can be ruled out entirely.
items.exp_text: Molecules at the surface of ice can gain enough energy from sunlight and dry air to break free directly into vapour, without first needing to become liquid. This process, sublimation, needs no rise above freezing at all, since it never asks the ice to melt in the first place. A snowbank can quietly shrink away on a freezing, sunny day, with nothing but dry air to show where the missing snow went.
